hypotheses.title: _addCredIdPerAddress and _removeCredIdPerAddress are public and unauthenticated
hypotheses.description: Both `_addCredIdPerAddress` and `_removeCredIdPerAddress` are declared `public` despite being internal helpers. Any external caller can invoke them with an arbitrary `sender_` address, corrupting `_credIdsPerAddress`, `_credIdsPerAddressCredIdIndex`, and `_credIdsPerAddressArrLength` for any user. This breaks `getPositionsForCurator` and the swap-and-pop bookkeeping used by `_updateCuratorShareBalance`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `_addCredIdPerAddress(credId, victim)` repeatedly to bloat the victim's array or push duplicate credIds. 2) Attacker calls `_removeCredIdPerAddress(credId, victim)` to pop entries and desync `_credIdsPerAddressCredIdIndex`. 3) Subsequent legitimate buys/sells by the victim revert or return wrong data.
hypotheses.impact: Corrupted per-user position accounting; `getPositionsForCurator` returns wrong results; legitimate trades can revert (DoS) or misreport holdings.
hypotheses.recommendation: Change visibility to `internal` (or `private`) so only `_updateCuratorShareBalance` can call them.

hypotheses.title: RewardControl.withdrawFor lets anyone drain another account's balance
hypotheses.description: `withdrawFor(address from, uint256 amount)` calls `_withdraw(from, from, amount)` with no check that `msg.sender == from` or that the caller is authorized. Any external caller can specify an arbitrary `from` address and withdraw that account's entire balance (or a specified amount) to `from`. There is no signature, allowance, or role check.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker identifies a victim with a positive `balanceOf` in PhiRewards. 2) Attacker calls `withdrawFor(victim, amount)` (or `amount = 0` for full balance). 3) `_withdraw` transfers ETH from the contract to `victim` — but the attacker can front-run or combine with other logic; more directly, the attacker can drain any account's balance to that account, and if the attacker controls `from` (e.g., a contract they own), they drain it to themselves.
hypotheses.impact: Any account's reward balance can be forcibly withdrawn by an untrusted caller; combined with attacker-controlled `from` addresses, funds are stolen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove `withdrawFor` or restrict it to `msg.sender == from` / an authorized operator with explicit approval.

hypotheses.title: getPositionsForCurator writes to wrong array indices
hypotheses.description: The loop iterates `i` from `start_` to `stopIndex` but writes results into `credIds[i]` and `amounts[i]` instead of `credIds[index]`/`amounts[index]`. When `start_ > 0`, this writes past the end of the freshly allocated arrays (length `stopIndex - start_`), corrupting memory, and leaves slots `[0, start_)` uninitialized. The `index` counter is incremented but never used as the write index.
hypotheses.attackPath: Any external caller invokes `getPositionsForCurator(curator, 1, N)` with `start_ > 0`. The out-of-bounds writes corrupt the returned arrays (and potentially adjacent memory), producing garbage credIds/amounts. Downstream consumers (e.g., CuratorRewardsDistributor or off-chain indexers) receive incorrect data.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting / corrupted return data; any integrator relying on this view for reward distribution or UI will compute incorrect positions.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `credIds[index] = credId; amounts[index] = amount;` and increment `index` after each write.

hypotheses.title: Anyone can call distribute() to drain curator rewards to themselves
hypotheses.description: `distribute(uint256 credId)` has no access control modifier, so any external caller can invoke it. The function computes `royaltyfee` and sends `royaltyfee + distributeAmount - actualDistributeAmount` to `_msgSender()`. Since `withdrawRoyalty` is 100 (1%) and rounding dust is also sent to the caller, an attacker can repeatedly call `distribute` on any cred with a balance and collect the royalty fee plus rounding remainder, which is intended for the protocol/owner.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a credId with a positive `balanceOf`. 2) Attacker calls `distribute(credId)` directly. 3) Contract transfers `royaltyfee + distributeAmount - actualDistributeAmount` to `msg.sender` (attacker). 4) Attacker repeats for every cred with balance.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of protocol royalty fees and rounding dust to any untrusted caller; the intended recipient (owner/protocol) never receives the royalty portion.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `onlyOwner` (or a dedicated distributor role) to `distribute`, or route the royalty fee to a fixed protocol address rather than `_msgSender()`.

hypotheses.title: CuratorRewardsDistributor.distribute sends royalty to _msgSender
hypotheses.description: `distribute` is permissionless and sends `royaltyfee + distributeAmount - actualDistributeAmount` to `_msgSender()`. Any external actor can call `distribute(credId)` and receive the royalty fee plus rounding dust. The royalty is intended for the protocol/owner, but any caller captures it.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker monitors `balanceOf[credId] > 0`, calls `distribute(credId)`, and receives `royaltyfee` (1% of totalBalance) plus rounding dust directly to their address.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of protocol royalty fees; attacker drains the royalty portion of every distribution.
hypotheses.recommendation: Send `royaltyfee` to a protocol-controlled address (e.g., `owner()` or a configured fee destination) instead of `_msgSender()`.

hypotheses.title: CuratorRewardsDistributor.distribute() sends refund to msg.sender, not protocol
hypotheses.description: Thematically the "dust" remainder `royaltyfee + distributeAmount - actualDistributeAmount` (including the protocol's royalty fee) is sent to `_msgSender()` rather than to the protocol or left in the contract. Since `distribute()` is external and permissionless, any caller can trigger distribution and pocket the royalty+dust. The royalty is intended as protocol revenue (`withdrawRoyalty`), yet it leaks to whoever calls `distribute()`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a cred with nonzero `balanceOf[credId]` accumulated by others. 2) Attacker calls `distribute(credId)` (permissionless). 3) `royaltyfee` (totalBalance * withdrawRoyalty / RATIO_BASE) plus rounding remainder `distributeAmount - actualDistributeAmount` is sent to attacker via `_msgSender().safeTransferETH(...)`. 4) Attacker collects protocol royalty and dust.
hypotheses.impact: The protocol loses its configured royalty on every curator reward distribution; a MEV/greedy caller siphons protocol funds. Anyone can grief proportional accounting of protocol revenue.
hypotheses.recommendation: Send `royaltyfee` to the protocol treasury/distributor contract (not msg.sender), and either keep the dust in the contract or forward to treasury.

hypotheses.title: _processClaim refunds to _msgSender which is factory in self-call
hypotheses.description: When `claim` is invoked via `this.claim{value: ...}` from `batchClaim`, `_msgSender()` inside `_processClaim` is the factory contract itself. The refund line `_msgSender().safeTransferETH(etherValue_ - mintFee)` sends excess ETH to the factory, not the user. Similarly, `protocolFeeDestination.safeTransferETH(mintProtocolFee * quantity_)` is fine, but the refund is lost to the user.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `batchClaim` with overpayment on any entry; the excess is refunded to the factory contract and later withdrawn by the owner to `protocolFeeDestination`.
hypotheses.impact: User funds lost to protocol.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track the original caller through the self-call (e.g., pass it as a parameter) and refund to that address.

hypotheses.title: PhiFactory.claim lacks nonReentrant allowing reentrancy via external claim
hypotheses.description: `claim()` is external payable and not protected by `nonReentrant`, yet it makes an external call to `this.merkleClaim`/`this.signatureClaim` which in turn calls `_processClaim` that forwards ETH to `art.artAddress` via a low-level call. The art contract's `claimFromFactory` calls `mint` which invokes `_mint` (ERC1155) and `handleRewardsAndGetValueSent` on PhiRewards, both of which can call back into the factory. Because `claim()` itself has no reentrancy guard, an attacker can re-enter `claim()` (or `batchClaim`) while the outer call is still executing.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious art contract (or uses a cred whose art contract they control) whose `claimFromFactory` re-enters `PhiFactory.claim` with the same or different artId. 2) Call `claim()` with encoded data pointing to that art. 3) During `_processClaim`'s low-level call to `art.artAddress`, the malicious contract re-enters `claim()`/`batchClaim()` before `art.numberMinted` and `artMinted` are finalized for the outer call. 4) Repeat to mint beyond `maxSupply` or double-claim rewards.
hypotheses.impact: Bypass of `maxSupply`/`artMinted` accounting, duplicate reward payouts, potential draining of PhiRewards balances.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `claim()` and `batchClaim()`, or restructure so state updates in `_validateAndUpdateClaimState` are finalized before any external call.

hypotheses.title: PhiNFT1155.createArtFromFactory refunds to msg.sender not payer
hypotheses.description: `createArtFromFactory` is called by `PhiFactory` via `newArt.call{value: msg.value}(...)`. Inside, `_msgSender()` is the PhiFactory contract, not the original caller. The refund `_msgSender().safeTransferETH(msg.value - artFee)` sends excess ETH back to the PhiFactory contract, not the user. The PhiFactory has a `withdraw()` that sends all balance to `protocolFeeDestination`, so user refunds are effectively donated to the protocol.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User calls `PhiFactory.createArt` with `msg.value > artCreateFee`. 2) PhiFactory forwards `msg.value` to `createArtFromFactory`. 3) Refund goes to PhiFactory, not the user. 4) PhiFactory owner later calls `withdraw()` and the excess is sent to `protocolFeeDestination`.
hypotheses.impact: Users lose excess ETH sent during art creation; funds are misdirected to the protocol.
hypotheses.recommendation: Have PhiFactory compute and refund excess to the original caller, or pass the payer address explicitly.

hypotheses.title: signatureClaim in PhiFactory does not bind signature to msg.sender
hypotheses.description: `signatureClaim` decodes `minter_` from `encodeData_` and verifies the signature over `keccak256(encodeData_)` against `phiSignerAddress`, but never checks that `minter_ == _msgSender()`. The `_validateAndUpdateClaimState` uses `minter_` for state updates, and `_processClaim` mints to `minter_`. Any third party who observes a valid signed claim (e.g., in the mempool) can submit it themselves, causing the mint to be attributed to the signed `minter_` while the attacker pays the fee — or, if the attacker substitutes their own address as `minter_`, the signature check fails, but the original signed payload can still be front-run to grief the intended minter.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim broadcasts a `signatureClaim` transaction with a valid signature. 2) Attacker sees it in the mempool, copies `signature_` and `encodeData_`, and submits with higher gas. 3) Attacker's tx executes first, minting to the victim's `minter_` address but consuming the victim's eligibility and the attacker's fee; victim's tx reverts or double-mints if not guarded.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing / denial of service for the intended minter; potential double-mint if `artMinted` is not checked per-minter (it is set, but `credMinted` is only set once, so a second claim by the same minter for a different art under the same cred is allowed).
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `minter_ == _msgSender()` in `signatureClaim`, or include `msg.sender` in the signed payload.

hypotheses.title: CuratorRewardsDistributor dust refund goes to untrusted caller
hypotheses.description: `distribute` computes `actualDistributeAmount` and sends `royaltyfee + distributeAmount - actualDistributeAmount` to `_msgSender()` rather than back to the depositor or back into `balanceOf[credId]`. Anyone can call `distribute(credId)`, so the caller captures the rounding dust and any per-user zero-reward remainder, plus the protocol `royaltyfee`. The royalty fee is supposed to be a protocol cut but is credited to the caller's address with no accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deposits a tiny amount (or simply monitors deposits) into a `credId`. 2. Attacker calls `distribute(credId)` first. 3. Contract computes `royaltyfee = totalBalance * withdrawRoyalty / 10000` and the rounding shortfall, and transfers `royaltyfee + distributeAmount - actualDistributeAmount` to the attacker. 4. Remaining `actualDistributeAmount` is pushed to `phiRewardsContract.depositBatch`. 5. Attacker repeats on every new deposit, harvesting the royalty cut and rounding remainder.
hypotheses.impact: Direct ETH theft from curator reward pools; protocol royalty never reaches the protocol; distribution becomes unfair to depositors because a permissionless caller pockets the difference.
hypotheses.recommendation: Send `royaltyfee` to a protocol-owned address (e.g., `protocolFeeDestination`) and refund `distributeAmount - actualDistributeAmount` back into `balanceOf[credId]` (or to the depositor who called `deposit`) instead of `_msgSender()`.

hypotheses.title: batchClaim forwards msg.value incorrectly to self.claim
hypotheses.description: `batchClaim` sums `ethValue_` and requires `msg.value == totalEthValue`, then loops calling `this.claim{value: ethValue_[i]}(...)`. Each `claim` call re-enters the factory with its own `msg.value`. Inside `claim`, `getArtMintFee` is computed and `this.merkleClaim{value: mintFee}` or `this.signatureClaim{value: mintFee}` is invoked. If `ethValue_[i]` is less than the actual `mintFee`, the inner call reverts. But if `ethValue_[i]` is greater, the excess is refunded to `_msgSender()` — which is the factory itself (since `this.claim` is called by the factory). The refund goes to the factory contract, not the original caller, and is later sweepable by `withdraw()` to `protocolFeeDestination`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `batchClaim` with `ethValue_[i]` larger than the required mint fee for some entries. The excess ETH is refunded to the factory contract address (via `_msgSender().safeTransferETH` where `_msgSender()` is the factory). The attacker loses that ETH to the protocol.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user funds — excess ETH is trapped in the factory and swept to `protocolFeeDestination`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Refund excess to the original caller (pass through `tx.origin` or track the outer caller), or require exact `ethValue_` per entry.

hypotheses.title: PhiNFT1155.initialize can be front-run to hijack ownership
hypotheses.description: `PhiNFT1155` is deployed via `cloneDeterministic` in `PhiFactory._createNewNFTContract`, and `initialize` is called immediately by the factory. However, the clone address is deterministic on `(block.chainid, newArtId, credId)`, and `initialize` is `external initializer` with no caller restriction. If the factory's `createArt` transaction is front-run or if the clone is deployed separately, an attacker can call `initialize` first, setting `__Ownable_init(msg.sender)` to themselves and `phiFactoryContract = msg.sender`. The factory's subsequent `initialize` call would revert (already initialized), and the attacker would own the NFT contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker predicts the clone address for a pending `createArt` (deterministic). 2) Attacker deploys the clone themselves (or front-runs the factory tx) and calls `initialize` with their own address as `msg.sender`. 3) Attacker becomes owner and sets `phiFactoryContract` to themselves. 4) Factory's `initialize` reverts; the art is unusable or controlled by attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker gains ownership of the NFT contract, can pause/unpause, upgrade (UUPS), and control `phiFactoryContract`, potentially stealing mint fees or bricking the art.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `initialize` to be callable only by the factory (e.g., `require(msg.sender == expectedFactory)`), or use `LibClone` with an atomic deploy+initialize pattern that cannot be front-run.

hypotheses.title: CuratorRewardsDistributor.distribute reverts on zero-amount recipients
hypotheses.description: `distribute()` builds `amounts[]` and `reasons[]` arrays sized to `distributeAddresses.length`, but only fills entries where `userRewards > 0`. It then calls `phiRewardsContract.depositBatch{value: actualDistributeAmount}(distributeAddresses, amounts, reasons, ...)`. In `RewardControl.depositBatch`, the loop sums `amounts[i]` and requires `msg.value == expectedTotalValue`. Since `actualDistributeAmount` equals the sum of the filled entries, this check passes, but the loop also emits a Deposit event for every recipient including zero-amount ones — that is fine. However, if any curator's share is so small that `userRewards == 0` (rounding), the entry stays zero and the deposit still succeeds. The real DoS: `distribute()` is permissionless and any caller can trigger it, but the royalty fee `royaltyfee + distributeAmount - actualDistributeAmount` is sent to `_msgSender()`. A griefer can call `distribute()` repeatedly to siphon the rounding dust, and more importantly, if `distributeAddresses` is large the loop can exceed block gas limits, permanently blocking distribution and locking `balanceOf[credId]` funds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits until a cred has many curators (or creates many tiny-share positions via `buyShareCred`). 2) Attacker calls `distribute(credId)`; the loop over `getCuratorAddresses(credId, 0, 0)` iterates all curators. 3) With enough curators, the transaction exceeds block gas limit and reverts. 4) Funds in `balanceOf[credId]` can never be distributed because every call reverts.
hypotheses.impact: Curator rewards permanently stuck in the distributor; royalty dust repeatedly captured by whoever calls `distribute()`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add pagination to `distribute()` (start/stop indices) and/or cap the number of curators processed per call; skip zero-amount recipients before building arrays.

hypotheses.title: Merkle claim leaf does not bind artId, enabling cross-art proof reuse
hypotheses.description: In `merkleClaim`, the leaf is computed as `keccak256(bytes.concat(keccak256(abi.encode(minter_, leafPart_))))` and verified against `credMerkleRoot[art.credChainId][art.credId]`. The `artId_` is decoded from `encodeData_` and used to look up the art, but the leaf itself does not include `artId_`. If two arts share the same `credChainId` and `credId` (which is possible because `credNFTContracts[credChainId][credId]` is reused across arts via `_useExistingNFTContract`), the same Merkle proof and `leafPart_` can be replayed against any art under that cred, minting multiple arts with a single proof.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid Merkle proof for cred (chainId, credId). 2) Attacker calls `merkleClaim` with `artId_` of a different art that shares the same `credChainId`/`credId`. 3) The proof verifies against the shared root, and `_validateAndUpdateClaimState` only checks `credMinted[credChainId][credId][minter_]` (which is set once) but still allows `artMinted[artId_][minter_]` and `art.numberMinted` to increment for the new art.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can mint unlimited arts under the same cred using one proof, draining mint fees/rewards and inflating supply.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `artId_` (or the NFT contract address) in the Merkle leaf so proofs are bound to a specific art.

hypotheses.title: _validateAndUpdateClaimState allows msg.sender == artAddress bypass
hypotheses.description: The check `if (tx.origin != _msgSender() && msg.sender != art.artAddress && msg.sender != address(this))` permits any call where `msg.sender == art.artAddress`. Since `art.artAddress` is a PhiNFT1155 clone whose `claimFromFactory` is `onlyPhiFactory`, this is intended for the internal call path. However, `signatureClaim` and `merkleClaim` are `external` and callable directly by anyone; the check only blocks when `tx.origin != _msgSender()`. A malicious contract can call `signatureClaim` on behalf of a victim (msg.sender = attacker contract, tx.origin = attacker EOA) — but the real issue is that `_msgSender()` in the factory is the direct caller, so `tx.origin != _msgSender()` is true and the check reverts. The bypass is that `msg.sender == address(this)` is allowed, meaning the factory's own `claim`/`batchClaim` self-calls pass. This is fine, but combined with `_processClaim` forwarding `msg.value` to the art contract, an attacker can craft a claim where `minter_` differs from `_msgSender()`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `signatureClaim` with a valid signature (obtained legitimately) but sets `minter_` to a victim address. `_validateAndUpdateClaimState` marks `artMinted[artId][victim] = true` and `credMinted[...][victim] = true`, consuming the victim's one-time mint slot. The NFT is minted to the victim, but the victim can never claim again.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing — victim's mint slot is consumed without their consent; they cannot claim the art themselves.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `minter_ == _msgSender()` in `signatureClaim`/`merkleClaim`, or bind the signature to `msg.sender`.

hypotheses.title: PhiFactory._processClaim refunds excess ETH to msg.sender (caller) instead of original payer in batchClaim
hypotheses.description: When a claim is submitted through `batchClaim` or via the NFT's `Claimable.signatureClaim()`/`merkleClaim()` proxies, `_msgSender()` is the direct caller (`address(this)` in the batch proxy case). `_processClaim` refunds `etherValue_ - mintFee` via `_msgSender().safeTransferETH(...)`. In batch flows `msg.sender` is the PhiFactory itself (via the `this.claim{value:...}` self-call), which is fine because PhiFactory holds no stray balance — but the outer refund of unused `msg.value` in `batchClaim` uses `msg.value - totalEthValue` which is validated as equal. The dangerous case is that `signatureClaim`/`merkleClaim` forward `msg.value` from the NFT contract's proxy — the NFT contract's `Claimable` forwards `msg.value` exactly, so refund returns to NFT contract, which has no forwarding mechanism → refund stuck. Attacker pattern: call `PhiNFT1155.merkleClaim` with overpayment; excess is refunded to PhiNFT1155 (address(this) at factory) which cannot forward it out. The NFT contract lacks a withdraw function, so excess ETH is permanently locked.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `PhiNFT1155.merkleClaim`/`signatureClaim` with `msg.value > mintFee`. 2) NFT's Claimable forwards `msg.value` to `PhiFactory.merkleClaim` with `address(this)=NFT`. 3) Factory `_processClaim` refunds `etherValue - mintFee` to `_msgSender()` which is PhiNFT1155. 4) NFT has no withdraw → ETH stuck in NFT contract.
hypotheses.impact: User ETH lost/stuck in NFT contract; no recovery path.
hypotheses.recommendation: In Claimable proxies, refactor so refunds return to the original EOA (or add a rescue) — e.g., in `_processClaim` refund to `tx.origin` when caller is a known art contract, or forward refund back through the proxy.

hypotheses.title: Cred._handleTrade sell path can be permanently blocked by share lock
hypotheses.description: On sell, `_handleTrade` requires `block.timestamp > lastTradeTimestamp[credId_][curator_] + SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD`. `lastTradeTimestamp` is set on every buy. A curator who buys and then wants to sell must wait 10 minutes. More critically, `_executeBatchTrade` for sells also checks this per cred. If a curator's `lastTradeTimestamp` is updated by a buy in the same block as a sell attempt (e.g., via a contract that buys then sells), the sell reverts. There is no admin override or emergency exit, so a curator whose position is locked by a malicious contract interaction cannot exit.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or a buggy integrator) triggers a buy on behalf of a victim curator via `buyShareCredFor`. 2) `lastTradeTimestamp[credId][victim]` is set to `block.timestamp`. 3) Victim cannot sell for 10 minutes; repeated buys by attacker can keep the lock active indefinitely, trapping the victim's shares.
hypotheses.impact: Victim's shares are frozen; they cannot exit their position while the attacker keeps buying on their behalf.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only update `lastTradeTimestamp` for the actual `_msgSender()` when they are the curator, or allow the curator to override the lock.

hypotheses.title: createArt signature does not bind chainId or contract address
hypotheses.description: `_validateArtCreationSignature` recovers the signer over `keccak256(signedData_)` and checks `expiresIn_ <= block.timestamp`, but `signedData_` is `abi.encode(uint256 expiresIn_, string uri_, bytes credData)` — it contains no `block.chainid` and no `address(this)`. A signature valid on one chain (or one deployment of PhiFactory) can be replayed on another chain where the same `phiSignerAddress` is configured, creating duplicate arts with the same cred data.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid `signedData_`/`signature_` pair from a legitimate art creation on chain A. 2) Attacker submits the same pair to `createArt` on chain B (or a forked deployment) where `phiSignerAddress` is the same. 3) The signature verifies, and a new art is created on chain B without the signer's intent.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized art creation on other chains, potential reward/fee misallocation, and duplicate creds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `block.chainid` and `address(this)` in the signed payload for `createArt`.

hypotheses.title: claim() and batchClaim() bypass whenNotPaused via self-call
hypotheses.description: `claim()` and `batchClaim()` are not guarded by `whenNotPaused`. They internally call `this.merkleClaim{...}` / `this.signatureClaim{...}`, which are guarded. However, `_validateAndUpdateClaimState` explicitly allows `msg.sender == address(this)`, and the outer `claim`/`batchClaim` entry points remain callable while paused. Because the inner call is made from the contract itself, the pause check on the inner function is the only barrier — but the outer functions themselves are reachable during pause, and any future refactor or direct path that reaches `_processClaim` without the inner guard would mint while paused. More concretely, the pause is intended to halt all minting, yet `claim`/`batchClaim` are not marked `whenNotPaused`, so the pause semantics are inconsistent and rely entirely on the inner call.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Owner pauses the factory. 2) Attacker calls `claim(encodeData)` or `batchClaim(...)`. 3) The outer function executes; the inner `this.signatureClaim`/`this.merkleClaim` reverts due to `whenNotPaused`, so the tx reverts — but the outer functions are still reachable and any state change before the inner call (none currently) would persist. If the inner guard is ever removed or a new branch is added, minting proceeds while paused.
hypotheses.impact: Inconsistent pause enforcement; potential minting during emergency pause if the inner guard is bypassed or refactored.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `whenNotPaused` to `claim()` and `batchClaim()` so the pause is enforced at every entry point.

hypotheses.title: CuratorRewardsDistributor.distribute uses stale share snapshot allowing reward dilution via front-run
hypotheses.description: `distribute` reads `credContract.getCuratorAddresses(credId, 0, 0)` and `getShareNumber` at execution time, then distributes `totalBalance` proportionally. An attacker who observes a pending `distribute` tx (or a large `deposit` to the distributor) can front-run by buying shares in the cred via `Cred.buyShareCred`, capturing a large share of the distribution, then sell after `SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD` (10 min). The distributor has no snapshot/epoch mechanism — rewards are split by current holdings at the moment `distribute` is called. This is classic reward-sniping.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sees `deposit(credId, X)` or pending `distribute(credId)`. 2) Attacker calls `Cred.buyShareCred(credId, largeAmount, maxPrice)` to acquire shares (paying curve price). 3) Attacker calls `CuratorRewardsDistributor.distribute(credId)` (or lets someone else). 4) Attacker receives proportional share of `totalBalance`. 5) After 10 min lock, attacker sells shares back. Profit if distribution share > curve cost + fees.
hypotheses.impact: Existing curators' rewards diluted; attacker extracts value from the distributor balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a snapshot (e.g., record balances at deposit time or use a checkpointed share accounting) so only pre-existing holders share the distribution.

hypotheses.title: Cred._handleTrade sends ETH before updating lastTradeTimestamp on sell
hypotheses.description: In the sell branch, `curator_.safeTransferETH(price - protocolFee - creatorFee)` is executed before `cred.latestActiveTimestamp = block.timestamp` and before the `Trade` event, but more importantly the share balance and supply are updated before the ETH send. However, `_handleTrade` is not `nonReentrant` (only `_executeBatchTrade` is). A malicious curator contract receiving ETH can re-enter `buyShareCred`/`sellShareCred`/`buyShareCredFor` during the ETH transfer, and since `lastTradeTimestamp` for the sell path is only set on buy, the SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD check can be bypassed on re-entry.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker buys shares to set `lastTradeTimestamp`. 2) Attacker calls `sellShareCred` from a contract whose `receive()` re-enters `sellShareCred` again. 3) The lock check `block.timestamp <= lastTradeTimestamp + SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD` is evaluated against the same timestamp, but the re-entrant call sees the already-decremented supply and can sell more shares within the lock window because the outer call's state changes are partially applied.
hypotheses.impact: Bypass of SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD anti-flash-trade protection, enabling same-block buy/sell arbitrage against the bonding curve.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `_handleTrade` (or to the public buy/sell entry points) and set `lastTradeTimestamp` before any ETH transfer.

hypotheses.title: PhiNFT1155.claimFromFactory mints before reward handling enabling reentrancy
hypotheses.description: `claimFromFactory` calls `mint(minter_, tokenId_, quantity_, ...)` which invokes `_mint` (ERC1155) — this triggers `onERC1155Received` on the recipient if it is a contract. Only after that does it call `IPhiRewards.handleRewardsAndGetValueSent`. A malicious minter contract can re-enter `claimFromFactory` (or the factory's `claim`) during the ERC1155 callback, before rewards are accounted, and before `art.numberMinted` is finalized in the factory's `_validateAndUpdateClaimState` (which runs before `_processClaim` but the factory's `claim` path is not guarded).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract that implements `onERC1155Received` to re-enter `PhiFactory.claim` or `PhiNFT1155.claimFromFactory`. 2) Call `claim` with attacker as minter. 3) During `_mint`, the callback re-enters and mints again before the outer call's reward accounting completes.
hypotheses.impact: Duplicate mints, reward accounting corruption, potential over-minting beyond maxSupply.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `_mint` (non-safe) or perform reward handling and state finalization before the ERC1155 callback, and add reentrancy guards on the factory claim paths.

hypotheses.title: PhiFactory.batchClaim loops over user array with external self-calls
hypotheses.description: `batchClaim` iterates over `encodeDatas_` and performs `this.claim{value: ethValue_[i]}(encodeDatas_[i])` for each entry. Each iteration is an external call that re-enters `claim`, which decompresses data, decodes, and calls `merkleClaim`/`signatureClaim` (also external self-calls). The gas cost per element is very high, and the array length is fully user-controlled with no cap. A caller can pass a large array to force out-of-gas reverts, but more importantly, a malicious `encodeDatas_` entry that reverts (e.g., invalid proof) reverts the entire batch, so a single bad entry blocks all legitimate claims in the same batch.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker submits a `batchClaim` with many entries where one entry is crafted to revert (e.g., expired signature or invalid merkle proof). 2) The whole batch reverts, wasting gas. 3) If any integrator relies on batchClaim for atomic multi-claim, they are griefed.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing of batch operations; no direct fund loss but blocks legitimate batched claims.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap `encodeDatas_.length` and/or use try/catch per element to skip failing claims.

hypotheses.title: PhiRewards.depositRewards sends curator reward to distributor without refund path
hypotheses.description: When `chainSync_` is true and `curatorRewardsDistributor` is set, `depositRewards` forwards `curateTotalReward_` to `curatorRewardsDistributor.deposit{value: curateTotalReward_}(credId_, curateTotalReward_)`. If the distributor's `credContract.isExist(credId_)` returns false (e.g., cred created on a different chain or not yet synced), the deposit reverts, which reverts the entire claim. There is no fallback to credit `balanceOf[receiver_]` in that case, so claims for such creds are permanently blocked.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A cred exists on chain A but the distributor on chain B has a different `credContract` that doesn't know the credId. 2) A claim on chain B with `chainSync_ = true` calls `depositRewards`, which calls `curatorRewardsDistributor.deposit` and reverts on `InvalidCredId`. 3) The claim cannot succeed; the minter's ETH is stuck in the reverted call (returned, but claim is blocked).
hypotheses.impact: Claims for cross-chain creds are permanently blocked; users cannot mint.
hypotheses.recommendation: Wrap the distributor deposit in a try/catch and fall back to crediting `balanceOf[receiver_]` on failure.

hypotheses.title: distribute() reverts when rounding produces zero per-user payout but keeps full balance
hypotheses.description: When `actualDistributeAmount == 0` but `totalBalance > 0` (large curator set, tiny balance, or high `withdrawRoyalty`), the function still zeroes `balanceOf[credId]` and forwards `royaltyfee + distributeAmount` to `_msgSender()`. The `depositBatch` call with `actualDistributeAmount = 0` and `depositBatch`'s `msg.value != expectedTotalValue` check would normally reject, but the loop short-circuits before that and the caller receives the entire balance. No per-user accounting is retained to ever allow those users to be paid; the funds are gone from `balanceOf[credId]` forever.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker funds a cred with many shareholders and a tiny balance so each `userRewards` rounds to 0. 2. Attacker calls `distribute(credId)`. 3. Loop yields `actualDistributeAmount = 0`; `balanceOf[credId] -= totalBalance` sets storage to 0; `_msgSender().safeTransferETH(royaltyfee + distributeAmount)` sweeps everything to the attacker (subject to any subsequent `depositBatch{value:0}` call which performs no ETH transfer). 4. Shareholders permanently cannot claim; the balance is erased.
hypotheses.impact: Deposited curator rewards are erased from accounting and swept to the caller while all eligible curators receive nothing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert (or revert the `balanceOf` decrement) when `actualDistributeAmount == 0`, and refund any undistributed remainder back into `balanceOf[credId]`.

hypotheses.title: merkleClaim accepts arbitrary quantity without per-cred quantity binding
hypotheses.description: `merkleClaim` verifies the Merkle leaf over `(minter_, leafPart_)` only; `quantity_` is taken from `MintArgs` and never cross-checked against the leaf or a per-cred cap. The only cap is `art.maxSupply`, which is shared across all minters and cred identities tied to that NFT contract. A single whitelisted minter can mint their entire allowed allocation up to `maxSupply` in one transaction, draining the art supply and any referral/verifier rewards tied to that minter's claim, and also consuming the shared token supply that belongs to other eligible minters on the same cred.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker is (or obtains) one Merkle-eligible leaf. 2. Attacker submits `merkleClaim` with `quantity_ = art.maxSupply` (or the largest allowed by supply). 3. `_validateAndUpdateClaimState` passes because `art.numberMinted + quantity_ <= maxSupply` and `credMinted[minter]` is only a boolean. 4. Attacker receives N units of the token, and referral/verifier rewards are credited N times via `handleRewardsAndGetValueSent`. 5. Other leaves cannot mint because supply is exhausted.
hypotheses.impact: Unfair allocation of a shared cred supply to a single minter; referral and verifier rewards multiplied by attacker-chosen quantity, draining PhiRewards balances allocated for legitimate claims.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind `quantity_` into the Merkle leaf (e.g., include the max allowed quantity per minter in the proof) or track cumulative minted per minter per art with a per-minter cap enforced in `_validateAndUpdateClaimState`.

hypotheses.title: _getCuratorData pagination uses wrong stop bound
hypotheses.description: The function treats `stop_` as an exclusive upper bound (`i < stopIndex`), but callers like `getCuratorAddresses(credId, 0, 0)` pass `0` meaning "all". When a caller passes `stop_ == shareBalance.length()`, the last curator is silently excluded. More importantly, `CuratorRewardsDistributor.distribute` calls `getCuratorAddresses(credId, 0, 0)` which is fine, but any caller passing an explicit `stop_` equal to length loses the last holder, causing reward distribution to skip them.
hypotheses.attackPath: An external caller (or the distributor if configured with explicit bounds) requests a page ending at `length`, and the last curator is omitted from the returned list. Their share is not counted in `totalNum`, so their reward share is redistributed to others.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong reward accounting; last curator loses rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Document `stop_` as exclusive and ensure callers pass `length` (or `length+1`) consistently, or change the semantics to inclusive.

hypotheses.title: PhiFactory.initialize lacks nonZeroAddress checks on critical addresses
hypotheses.description: `initialize` sets `phiSignerAddress`, `protocolFeeDestination`, `erc1155ArtAddress`, and `phiRewardsAddress` without zero-address validation. If any is left as `address(0)` (e.g., due to a deployment script bug or a front-run initializer), signature verification (`_recoverSigner(...) != phiSignerAddress`) would compare against `address(0)`, and `ECDSA.recover` returning `address(0)` on invalid signatures would pass the check, allowing anyone to forge signatures. Similarly, `protocolFeeDestination.safeTransferETH` would revert or send to zero.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) If `phiSignerAddress` is `address(0)` (misconfiguration or front-run), attacker submits any `signedData`/`signature` where `ECDSA.recover` returns `address(0)` (e.g., malformed signature). 2) `_validateArtCreationSignature` passes because `address(0) == phiSignerAddress`. 3) Attacker creates arbitrary arts or claims without a valid signer.
hypotheses.impact: Signature checks bypassed; unauthorized art creation and claims; potential loss of protocol fees.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonZeroAddress` checks for `phiSignerAddress_`, `protocolFeeDestination_`, `erc1155ArtAddress_`, and `phiRewardsAddress_` in `initialize`.

hypotheses.title: Cred.getCredSellPrice underflows for amount > currentSupply
hypotheses.description: `getCredSellPrice` calls `getPrice(currentSupply - amount_, amount_)` with an unchecked subtraction expressed via Solidity 0.8 revert (so it reverts), whereas the on-chain sell path in `_handleTrade` uses `price = ...` differently. Worse, `BondingCurve.getPrice` computes `_curve((supply_ + amount_)*1e18) - _curve(supply_*1e18)`; on a sell with `supply_ - amount_` correctly passed, the two `_curve` calls produce a negative difference subtracted — but `_curve` itself can revert or produce differences that don't match `getPriceData`'s sell branch (which passes `supply_-amount_` to `getPrice`). The public view returns different numbers than the actual sell path, misleading integrators and enabling price-limit miscalculation in downstream consumers.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted integrator/EOA uses `getCredSellPrice` to compute slippage bounds; the returned value mismatches the value used inside `_handleTrade`/`getPriceData`, allowing trades to revert or to bypass `minPrice_` checks in third-party flows. Also, a caller with `amount_ > currentSupply` gets a revert where the contract should return 0/revert explicitly.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect view accounting; integration/front-end mispricing; potential inconsistent fills.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make `getCredSellPrice` mirror `getPriceData`'s computation exactly (`getPrice(supply - amount, amount)` with supply check) and validate `amount_ <= currentSupply`.

hypotheses.title: PhiFactory.getArtMintFee uses mintProtocolFee as flat per-quantity fee, not percentage
hypotheses.description: `getArtMintFee` returns `IPhiRewards.computeMintReward(quantity_, mintFee) + quantity_ * mintProtocolFee`. `mintProtocolFee` is documented as "protocol fee percentage (in basis points)" and `setProtocolFee` caps it at 10_000. But it's multiplied directly by `quantity_` as if it were an absolute wei amount per token, not a percentage of `mintFee`. So a "1% fee" (100 bps) becomes 100 wei per token, and a "100% fee" (10_000) becomes 10_000 wei per token — completely decoupled from the actual mint fee. This means the protocol fee is essentially a fixed tiny wei amount regardless of art price, and `_processClaim` sends `mintProtocolFee * quantity_` to `protocolFeeDestination` while the rest goes to the art contract. Users pay `getArtMintFee` which includes this mis-scaled fee. Not directly exploitable for profit but breaks fee accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: N/A (accounting bug, not attacker-profitable directly)
hypotheses.impact: Protocol under-collects fees; users over/under-pay depending on mintFee magnitude.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute protocol fee as `(mintFee * quantity_ * mintProtocolFee) / 10_000` or clarify units.

hypotheses.title: CuratorRewardsDistributor.distribute reentrancy via ETH transfer before depositBatch
hypotheses.description: `distribute()` updates `balanceOf[credId] -= totalBalance` before calling `_msgSender().safeTransferETH(...)` and `phiRewardsContract.depositBatch{value: ...}`. The ETH transfer to `_msgSender()` can re-enter `distribute()` for the same credId. Since `balanceOf[credId]` was already zeroed, the re-entrant call reverts with `NoBalanceToDistribute`, but the attacker can re-enter `deposit()` to inflate balance and then re-enter `distribute()` again, or re-enter `distribute` for a different credId where they are a curator, manipulating share accounting mid-distribution.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is a curator of credId A and credId B. 2) Call `distribute(A)`; during the ETH transfer to attacker, re-enter `distribute(B)`. 3) Because `getCuratorAddresses` and `getShareNumber` are read live, the attacker can manipulate share balances (via re-entrant buy/sell in Cred) between the two distributions to skew reward allocation.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect reward distribution, potential over-payment to attacker-controlled curators.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to `distribute()` and perform all state reads/updates before external calls.

hypotheses.title: PhiFactory._processClaim refunds excess ETH before external call
hypotheses.description: `_processClaim` refunds excess ETH to `_msgSender()` via `safeTransferETH` before calling `art.artAddress.call{value: ...}`. A malicious `_msgSender()` contract can re-enter `claim`/`signatureClaim`/`merkleClaim` during the refund transfer. Although `_validateAndUpdateClaimState` runs before `_processClaim`, the re-entrant call will re-validate against the already-updated `art.numberMinted` and `artMinted`, but the outer call's `_processClaim` has not yet forwarded the mint fee to the art contract, so the attacker can cause the art contract to be called multiple times with the same `msg.value` accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `signatureClaim` with `msg.value` greater than the mint fee. 2) During the refund `safeTransferETH`, attacker's `receive()` re-enters `signatureClaim` with the same signature (still valid) and a fresh `msg.value`. 3) The re-entrant call passes validation because `artMinted` is set but the check is `if (!credMinted[...])` — it only sets, doesn't revert on already-minted, so multiple mints per minter are allowed.
hypotheses.impact: Multiple mints per minter per art, exceeding intended per-minter limits and draining rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move the refund after the external call, or add `nonReentrant` to the claim entry points.

hypotheses.title: Signature claim lacks chainId binding in Claimable.signatureClaim
hypotheses.description: The `signatureClaim()` helper builds `claimData_ = abi.encode(expiresIn_, minter_, ref_, verifier_, artId, block.chainid, data_)` and forwards it to `PhiFactory.signatureClaim`, which recovers the signer over `keccak256(encodeData_)`. However, the `artId` is derived from `getFactoryArtId(tokenId_)` on the local NFT contract, and the same `tokenId_`/`artId` mapping can exist on multiple chains (deterministic clone addresses via `keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.chainid, newArtId, credId))` differ, but the factory's `artIdCounter` and `artId` values are not chain-unique). More importantly, the `Claimable.signatureClaim` path is a public entrypoint that any user can call directly on the NFT contract, and the signature is verified only against `phiSignerAddress` in the factory — the `block.chainid` is included in the signed payload, but the NFT contract's `signatureClaim` does not enforce that the caller's `tokenId_` corresponds to the same `artId` that the signer intended, allowing a signature valid for one art to be replayed against a different art on the same chain if the signer's payload is reused.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a valid signed `claimData_` for art A. 2) Attacker calls `PhiNFT1155.signatureClaim()` (or `Claimable.signatureClaim`) with a `tokenId_` that maps to a different art B whose `artId` happens to match the signed `artId` (or reuses the same signature on a forked/duplicated deployment). 3) The factory recovers the signer over the attacker-supplied `encodeData_` and, if it matches, mints against the attacker-chosen art.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized minting of art tokens, bypassing intended eligibility, and potential reward misattribution.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the signature to the specific NFT contract address and tokenId, and verify the recovered signer against the exact `artId`/`tokenId` pair intended by the signer.

hypotheses.title: Cred creation self-buys first share with protocol/creator fees ignored
hypotheses.description: `_createCredInternal` calls `buyShareCred(credIdCounter, 1, 0)` without forwarding ETH. The buy path computes `price + protocolFee + creatorFee` and requires `msg.value >= price + protocolFee + creatorFee`. Since `msg.value` is zero at that call, if any of those fees are non-zero (protocolFeePercent > 0, or initial royalty > 0) the call reverts, but if they evaluate to zero (protocolFeePercent=0, buyShareRoyalty=0), the first share is minted for free to the creator. An untrusted creator can set `buyShareRoyalty_=0` and, on a chain where protocolFeePercent is 0, mint the genesis share with no payment, then dump it later at a price that includes the bonding-curve appreciation.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker calls `createCred` with `buyShareRoyalty_=0`, `sellShareRoyalty_=0` and a whitelisted bonding curve. 2. `_createCredInternal` invokes `buyShareCred(id, 1, 0)` with no ETH; because fees are zero, it passes. 3. Attacker now holds 1 share whose cost was zero, while the curve's `currentSupply` already advanced to 1. 4. Attacker waits `SHARE_LOCK_PERIOD` and sells via `sellShareCred`, receiving `price - protocolFee - creatorFee` where `price = getPrice(0,1)`. 5. Net gain is the genesis curve price for free, paid from the next buyer's deposits.
hypotheses.impact: Free extraction of the initial bonding-curve value from subsequent buyers; protocol loses solvency margin on every cred issuance when fee params are zero, and the cred creator can grind out free shares.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `msg.value >= getBuyPriceWithFee(credIdCounter, 1)` at creation time (or force the creator to pay the computed buy price explicitly) instead of unconditionally calling the free `buyShareCred`.

hypotheses.title: batchClaim loops external self-calls allowing partial-fee griefing
hypotheses.description: `batchClaim` verifies `msg.value == sum(ethValue_)` then loops `this.claim{value: ethValue_[i]}`, but `claim` may pay out less than `ethValue_[i]` if the encoded `quantity_` in the payload is smaller than the value passed (surplus is refunded inside `_processClaim` to `_msgSender()`, which is the factory itself during the self-call). Refunds sent to the factory during the loop accumulate in the factory and become claimable via `withdraw()` (owner) or silently lost to the caller — the caller's `ethValue_` always matches the sum, but per-claim `quantity_` is chosen by the attacker and can be set to 0 (revert) or to a smaller amount so the surplus stays in the factory. An attacker can craft a batch where `ethValue_[i]` exceeds the actual fee for claim `i` and then a later message value... but `_processClaim` refunds to `_msgSender()`, i.e., the factory contract during the self-call.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker builds `encodeDatas_` where each entry has `quantity_` less than `ethValue_[i]` implies. 2. Caller sends `msg.value == sum(ethValue_)`. 3. Each inner `this.claim{value: ethValue_[i]}` sees `msg.value >= getArtMintFee(...)` (true because attacker picked the value), refunds `ethValue_[i] - mintFee` to `_msgSender()`, which is the factory contract (self). 4. Surplus accumulates in the factory, later drainable only by owner via `withdraw()`, or locked. Caller retains no benefit unless they also know `quantity_` exactly, but the accounting is silently distorted.
hypotheses.impact: User funds swept into factory balance and only recoverable by owner; surplus ETH is permanently lost to non-owner callers, effectively donating to the protocol owner unexpectedly.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `_processClaim`, refund to `tx.origin`? (no) — better: `batchClaim` should compute and forward exactly `getArtMintFee` per entry, replacing `ethValue_[i]` with the required fee and refunding the difference to `_msgSender()` (the outer caller) rather than the factory.

hypotheses.title: Cred.batchBuyShareCred refund after batch execution enables reentrancy
hypotheses.description: `batchBuyShareCred` calls `_executeBatchBuy` (which is `nonReentrant`) and then refunds excess ETH to `_msgSender()` via `safeTransferETH`. The refund happens after the `nonReentrant` guard is released, so a malicious `_msgSender()` can re-enter `batchBuyShareCred` or `buyShareCred` during the refund. Since `_executeBatchTrade` already updated supplies and balances, the re-entrant call operates on consistent state, but the attacker can chain multiple batch buys within the same transaction to manipulate the bonding curve price for subsequent buys.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `batchBuyShareCred` with `msg.value` > totalCost. 2) During the refund transfer, re-enter `batchBuyShareCred` with a new set of credIds. 3) The re-entrant call sees updated supplies and can exploit price differences.
hypotheses.impact: Same-block price manipulation, potential arbitrage against the bonding curve.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move the refund before `_executeBatchBuy` or wrap the entire function in `nonReentrant`.

hypotheses.title: Mint rewards can be overpaid into PhiRewards and silently kept
hypotheses.description: `_processClaim` computes `mintFee = getArtMintFee(artId_, quantity_)`, refunds any excess ETH above `mintFee` to `_msgSender()`, and forwards `mintFee - mintProtocolFee * quantity_` to the NFT contract. That forwarded amount equals `IPhiRewards.computeMintReward(quantity_, arts[artId_].mintFee_)`. Any divergence between `mintFee` computed via `getArtMintFee` and the recipient's `computeMintReward` (e.g., if the PhiRewards reward parameters change between `_validateAndUpdateClaimState` and `handleRewardsAndGetValueSent` within the same tx — not possible, but with a stale/incorrect `mintFee` mismatch driven by admin parameter changes between transactions) leads to either a revert or overpayment stuck in `PhiRewards`. Because `handleRewardsAndGetValueSent` computes its own `computeMintReward` and credits balances by `quantity_ * (mintFee_ + artistReward)` etc., any surplus `msg.value` above that distribution is added to `balanceOf` of the reward addressees but the ETH itself stays in `PhiRewards` contract without a matching obligation on `totalSupply` reconciliation — `balanceOf` sum can exceed actual ETH, causing future `withdraw` to fail for the last claimant.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Admin raises `artistReward` (or similar) via `updateArtistReward`. 2. A previously quoted `getArtMintFee` (used by an integration) no longer matches `computeMintReward`. In the pull path, `_processClaim` forwards `mintFee - protocolFee*quantity_` and requirement `msg.value >= mintFee` still holds, but the PhiRewards-side accounting `quantity_ * (mintFee_ + artistReward + ...)` may exceed the forwarded amount, allowing the tx to revert, or if `mintFee` is under-quoted the receiver gets more than forwarded. 3. Persistent mismatch lets early claimers withdraw full balances while later ones have insufficient ETH backing.
hypotheses.impact: Reward accounting (`balanceOf`) can drift from actual ETH held; the last withdrawers face failed `withdraw`/`withdrawFor` calls (DoS on claiming earned rewards).
hypotheses.recommendation: Make PhiFactory push exactly `IPhiRewards.computeMintReward(quantity_, mintFee_)` and derive `mintProtocolFee` independently; or assert equality when forwarding so mismatches revert rather than accumulate.
